stories.topic: Ryan, the push-ups, and a deliberate post-hoc fallacy
stories.summary: In the late 1980s and early 1990s at Ferguson College, Pune, Amit was so thin you could count his ribs. Fresh from a boys' school and in an arts class that was about 80% girls, he chose between the canteen and the tapri based on the wind, so his shirt would not blow against his ribs. Gyms were not yet part of the culture. His consolation was Ryan, a devout Christian who was just as thin. Then one day, through Ryan's open hostel door, Amit saw him doing push-ups. Ryan explained that masturbation was a sin, and he had set himself 25 push-ups as the penance for each time. Six months later Ryan was buff, a 'Greek god', and Amit was the only one left with visible ribs. When another hostel friend (Amit gives him a pseudonym, Varun) quietly asked how to get a body like Ryan's, Amit told him, deliberately and as a joke: you have to masturbate.
stories.insight: This is post hoc ergo propter hoc in its purest form. One thing happened, then another, so the first must have caused the second. The joke works because the real cause, the push-ups, was hidden inside the sequence. Many of our causal stories leave out the hidden middle step in the same way.
stories.quote: The lesson here is that deliberately out of a sense of humor, I committed a fallacy called the post hoc ergo propter hoc.

stories.topic: The witch doctor's coat and the flooding Nile
stories.summary: A witch doctor claims that every spring he takes off his coat, and then the Nile floods, so the river must be responding to his coat. The sequence is real: spring, then coat, then flood. The causal claim is absurd. Ajay adds a thought experiment. If pressing a button gives you a biscuit one second later, two or three tries convince you that you caused it. Stretch the delay to 10 seconds and it gets harder. At 10 hours the mind can no longer connect the two.
stories.insight: Our sense of causality was built for a simple world of tigers and deer, where effects follow causes quickly. Today's information environment is far more complex, and many important processes play out over long timescales. So we have to lean on evidence and data rather than gut feel.
stories.quote: The witch doctor would claim that in spring, I take off my coat, and then the Nile floods. So the Nile responds to my action on the coat.

stories.topic: The coin in the crowded swimming pool
stories.summary: Amit recalls a metaphor from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who he thinks may have been quoting Don Boudreaux. Does dropping a coin into water raise the water level? In a lab, with a beaker and everything controlled, the answer is easy. Now try it in a huge, crowded swimming pool where people are splashing, it is windy and it is raining. The data will mostly be garbage. Amit says this is why economists love the post-war splits of North and South Korea and East and West Germany. They come close to a controlled experiment on free markets, and 'spoiler alert, free markets won'.
stories.insight: Social science happens in the swimming pool, not the beaker. Real controlled experiments are rare, and confirmation bias fills the gap. So claims that X caused Y deserve humility and caution.
stories.quote: Now imagine you are doing this in a crowded swimming pool. It's a big swimming pool, it is incredibly crowded, people are splashing around in it, it is windy and it is raining at the same time.

stories.topic: What really caused the Great Depression?
stories.summary: The standard story is that the 1929 stock market crash caused the Great Depression. Drawing on Thomas Sowell, Amit points out that unemployment in the months after the crash peaked at about 9% and was down to around 6.5% by June 1930. Then the government began to intervene, starting with the Smoot-Hawley tariff and followed by a series of other interventions, and things exploded. Sowell also notes a later stock market crash that was followed by decades of strong growth. Amit adds that he thinks Amity Shlaes has a book making a similar case.
stories.insight: A dramatic event followed by a disaster makes an easy causal story. The less visible chain of policy decisions in between can matter far more. Blaming the obvious trigger is a post-hoc fallacy at the scale of history.
stories.quote: It wasn't the stock market crash. It was a whole bunch of interventions which led to the problem.

stories.topic: The tomato glut and the coming chip glut
stories.summary: When tomatoes are scarce, a farmer reasons that he should plant tomatoes, spend heavily on inputs and make a killing. That is sensible for one farmer. But a million farmers respond to the same prices, the market floods, prices collapse to zero, and angry farmers dump truckloads of tomatoes on the roadside because transporting them isn't worth it. Ajay sees the same pattern with semiconductors: after the chip shortage, 'every idiot in the world' decided to build a fab. He predicts a glut and bankruptcies among chipmakers within a year or two.
stories.insight: This is the fallacy of composition in action. What is rational for one actor can be ruinous when everyone does it. The disciplined question is always: what happens if everybody does this?
stories.quote: What may be true for me in the small doesn't work when a million people think the same.

stories.topic: The dart-throwing monkey and the Infosys IPO
stories.summary: In finance it is well accepted that a monkey throwing darts builds a decent portfolio, and that nearly all clever humans picking stocks underperform it. Yet each of us thinks we are in the elite 0.01%. Ajay extends this to careers. Nobody could have predicted the software boom from the mid-90s, and the Infosys IPO was mostly undersubscribed. Insiders in a booming industry then credit their success to their own decisions. The honest test is to ask how you would have done if you had simply bought shares in 10 companies in your industry and done nothing. Only the outperformance over that baseline is yours.
stories.insight: Much of 'success' comes from the luck of being in software rather than seafood. Separate the industry tailwind from your own contribution before crediting the CEO, or yourself.
stories.quote: The world, the society attributes all firm success to the CEO, and I think that is wrong.

recommendations.item: Economic Facts and Fallacies
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: The framework for the whole episode. Its opening chapters lay out the five foundational fallacies the hosts discuss.
recommendations.reason: Sowell is one of Amit's intellectual heroes, 'still going strong at ninety plus'. The book names fallacies that are foundational, in that many other errors grow out of them. Understanding these frailties makes our thinking clearer.

recommendations.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Used to rebut the zero-sum fallacy. Stossel is 'one of my favorite columnists ever'.
recommendations.reason: When you buy coffee, both you and the seller say thank you because both are better off. It is the simplest illustration that voluntary exchange is positive-sum.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited for its chart of world GDP, flat for centuries and then shooting up.
recommendations.reason: It shows that as industrialisation, travel and free markets multiplied double thank-you moments, value and innovation exploded. This is the economic history behind the positive-sum world.

recommendations.item: Profit = Philanthropy
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The column behind Amit's line that the pursuit of profit is the greatest form of philanthropy.
recommendations.reason: In a world of voluntary exchange, the only way to profit is by making someone else better off. Profit is therefore an incentive to do good for others.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The column Amit links when he jokingly names a law of economics after himself.
recommendations.reason: It uses tariffs to show that interfering with free markets usually redistributes wealth from poor consumers to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the interference.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Cooperation
recommendations.creator: Robert Axelrod
recommendations.context: Raised after Amit argued for generosity over crabby, zero-sum behaviour in personal life.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'a fabulous book'. It formalises the optimal response to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever. Some punishment is optimal, grudges are not. That is very different from the behaviour of warlike tribes.

recommendations.item: Tim Urban's tweet on getting to know people
recommendations.creator: Tim Urban
recommendations.context: Read out while discussing the danger of judging individuals by their group, or by one opinion.
recommendations.reason: 'Whenever I get to know someone who seems perfect, I end up disappointed. Whenever I get to know someone who I think is the worst of the worst, I'm pleasantly surprised. Angels and demons aren't real.' It is a reminder to judge people less and stay open to them.

recommendations.item: The Day Ryan Started Masturbating
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as the written version of the college story Amit tells to explain the post-hoc fallacy.
recommendations.reason: It is the full telling of the episode's funniest illustration of mistaking sequence for causation.

recommendations.item: 'Wet streets cause rain' (Michael Crichton on Gell-Mann Amnesia)
recommendations.creator: Michael Crichton
recommendations.context: Amit borrows Crichton's phrase for getting causation backwards.
recommendations.reason: It is a memorable label for reverse causation: you see wet streets and rain together and conclude the streets caused the rain.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Man
recommendations.creator: Amity Shlaes
recommendations.context: Mentioned ('if I remember correctly') as also arguing that the 1929 crash alone did not cause the Great Depression.
recommendations.reason: It supports Sowell's case that government interventions, not the stock market crash, turned a downturn into a depression.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while drawing the personal lesson from the post-hoc fallacy.
recommendations.reason: Most of what happens to us is sheer dumb luck. Don't let success go to your head or failure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

recommendations.item: The Man of System (excerpted from The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a 'brilliant passage' and the origin of the chess-pieces fallacy.
recommendations.reason: It is the classic statement of the arrogance of imagining society as pieces on a chessboard that a planner can move at will.

recommendations.item: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Cited as Hayek's name for the chess-pieces fallacy.
recommendations.reason: Hayek's 'fatal conceit' is the belief that we can control a complex world from the top down. Beyond a certain level of complexity, no one has the information to do so.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Referred to as 'Hayek's great essay' while explaining spontaneous order.
recommendations.reason: It is the foundation for understanding why order can emerge without a top-down plan, and why central planners can never gather all the knowledge they need.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: 'An episode I really love', where the hosts discussed Hayek's essay and spontaneous order.
recommendations.reason: A deeper dive into the ideas behind the chess-pieces fallacy.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned by Ajay while giving the tomato-glut example of the fallacy of composition.
recommendations.reason: The earlier episode covered how farmers chasing the same high prices produce gluts and collapsing prices.

recommendations.item: The Selfish Gene
recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Ajay says the chess-pieces fallacy 'goes all the way to selfish gene'.
recommendations.reason: Every organism optimises for itself, so you can never suppress each person's drive to pursue their own life, liberty and happiness. That is why top-down control keeps failing.

recommendations.item: Untitled
recommendations.creator: Leonard Cohen
recommendations.context: 'I can't resist recommending' it. Ajay used it as an epigraph at the end of the technology-policy chapter of his book with Vijay Kelkar.
recommendations.reason: It is a slave speaking, saying that any system you design without us will not work. A poetic version of why top-down designs fail.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as 'the Kelkar and Shah book', where the Leonard Cohen poem serves as an epigraph to the technology-policy chapter.
recommendations.reason: It is Ajay's own treatment of economic policy, in which the limits of top-down system design are a recurring theme.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled during the open-ended fallacy: 'we have done an episode in the past' on how every act of government is an act of violence.
recommendations.reason: The state acts through coercion, starting with taxation. That makes every government rupee carry an opportunity cost.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points to 'our pair of episodes' on when the state should act and what it should do.
recommendations.reason: It brings two big ideas to policy: the no-free-lunch budget constraint, and the fact that coercive power has no such constraint.

recommendations.item: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked when Ajay argued that Indian health policy should shift from healthcare to public health.
recommendations.reason: Ajay explains in detail there why prevention beats cure, and why the distinction between public health and healthcare matters.

recommendations.item: Declutter (Episode 30 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit thinks they discussed the personal side of the open-ended fallacy there.
recommendations.reason: It covers recognising the constraints in our own lives, especially time, and prioritising accordingly.

recommendations.item: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
recommendations.creator: Christopher Blattman
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the week, prompted by Amit opening the episode by asking why we fight.
recommendations.reason: Ajay is glad an economist has 'opened the box of violence'. Taming violence, both between citizens and between state and citizens, is central to the development story, and economists usually stick to money and markets.

recommendations.item: The Three Languages of Politics
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation for the week, on the theme of why we fight.
recommendations.reason: It is a slim book you can read in an hour. Kling shows that ideological tribes talk past each other because they start from different core values: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians. Recognising the other side's value is the way to find common ground.

recommendations.item: In My Tribe
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside the book. Kling 'used to be a great blogger' and now has a newsletter 'you must subscribe to'.
recommendations.reason: It continues Kling's thinking, and Amit recalls a follow-up there or elsewhere that adds nuance to the three-languages framework.

recommendations.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay connects Kling's framework to the 'wolves and sheep' theme of that episode.
recommendations.reason: The sheep come in three flocks with different values, but all of them share an overarching interest in not being trampled by the wolves.

core_ideas.concept: Stone Age brains in a modern world
core_ideas.explanation: The world is too complex to grasp, so we make sense of it through simple stories. Those stories clash with each other, and sometimes all of them clash with reality. Our instincts were forged for small hunter-gatherer tribes. Ajay adds that the roughly 4,000 generations of modern humans are too few to change that 'hardware'. Many fallacies are instincts that once worked and now misfire.
core_ideas.quote: From a hundred thousand years ago to today, the period of modern man is a mere 4,000 generations, which is not enough to materially move the needle on our hardware.

core_ideas.concept: Why we disagree: facts, values and the reasoning engine
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's triad. We reason from facts (skewed by overweighting personal experience), from values (partly our birthright, often muddled), and through a reasoning engine. Disagreement comes from a difference in one of the three. The hope is that the reasoning engine, meaning logic, argument and proof, can be common ground for a shared notion of truth.
core_ideas.quote: Maybe there are certain universal stories of logic, of argument, of proof, which we can all agree on, and we can construct a social shared notion of truth.

core_ideas.explanation: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk I take is one you can't have. Modern exchange is different: voluntary transactions leave both sides better off. Zero-sum thinking drives statism and the confusion of inequality with poverty. Since 1991, hundreds of millions of Indians have left poverty even as inequality rose. Treating the economy as a fixed pie favours redistribution over growth and wrecks incentives. On a personal level, Amit argues against crabby scarcity thinking and for generosity, because someone else's success is not your loss.
core_ideas.quote: In a world of double thank you moments, the only way that I can profit is by making you better off.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge is the greatest positive-sum game
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's extension of the zero-sum argument. Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were created in some corner, and everyone got better off. The inventors of the transistor did not gain at our expense. Accumulated human knowledge is a public good whose spillovers transform everything.
core_ideas.quote: The emergence of culture and the development of knowledge is just a public good and it spills over, it inflects everything, and it is the greatest positive sum game story of the world.

core_ideas.concept: Intervention redistributes from the poor to the rich
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's self-named 'law'. Interfering with free markets usually transfers wealth upward. With tariffs, competition shrinks and ordinary consumers pay more or get less. The value they lose goes to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the tariff.
core_ideas.quote: Most interference in free markets leads to a redistribution from the poor to the rich.

core_ideas.explanation: This is the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for society, which is really robbing Peter to pay Paul. Ajay sees it as the core difference between thinking like a firm and thinking about an economy. Exporting more makes sense for one company, but using state power to subsidise land, electricity or the exchange rate so that every company exports can unbalance the economy. The test to always apply is: what if everyone does it?
core_ideas.quote: A baseball fan at a ballpark can see the game better by standing up. But if all the fans stand up, they will not all see better.

core_ideas.concept: The flip side: don't judge individuals by their group
core_ideas.explanation: Amit inverts the fallacy of composition. Stereotyping takes a trait attributed to a group, or seen in one member, and paints every individual with it. One sociopathic economist doesn't make all economists sociopaths. The same applies to condemning someone as evil over a single disagreement on social media. People regress to the mean: neither angels nor demons.
core_ideas.quote: We are all human, we are all frail, and we are all beautiful.

core_ideas.concept: A country is not a company
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay previews a future episode. Successful businesspeople assume their skills carry over to government, but they mostly don't, for two reasons. First, economy-wide actions trigger composition effects that a single firm never faces. Second, government wields coercive power, which firms largely lack.
core_ideas.quote: In a firm, you don't have much coercive power. Whereas when you're a government, you are dealing with the poison every day of coercive power.

core_ideas.concept: The post-hoc fallacy and its cousins
core_ideas.explanation: The post-hoc fallacy assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Its cousin, cum hoc ergo propter hoc, assumes that two simultaneous events must be causally linked. Michael Crichton's 'wet streets cause rain' gets the arrow backwards. These made sense in a simple world where a rustle in the bush meant a tiger. Amit argues that religion and ritual grew from such simple causal stories, for example about what causes rain. In a complex world they mislead us constantly, especially in economics.
core_ideas.quote: Something happened, something happened after it. Therefore the first thing caused the second thing.

core_ideas.concept: Our causal radar has a short range
core_ideas.explanation: If the biscuit arrives one second after the button press, we see causality instantly. If it arrives 10 hours later, we are lost. Many processes in the universe play out over long timescales, exactly where our intuition fails. So we must push harder to be evidence-based before making causal claims.
core_ideas.quote: The human mind is congenitally unable to see cause and effect playing out across longer timescales.

core_ideas.concept: Luck dominates, so judge yourself against the baseline
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's personal lesson: most of what happens to us is luck. Don't build stories like 'I am good, so good things happened' or 'I am bad, so bad things happened'. Keep doing the right thing, your dharma. Ajay's version for firms is to compare your results with simply holding your industry's stocks. Only the outperformance is your contribution.
core_ideas.quote: 98% of what happens to each of us is sheer dumb luck.

core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith's 'man of system' and Hayek's 'fatal conceit' describe the belief that society is a static chessboard a planner can arrange. Top-down control works for a tribe or a 10-person family firm. At scale, no one has the information, and spontaneous order emerges from 'human action, but not human design'. Amit says millions of Indians stayed poor longer than they should have because planners did not trust people's ingenuity. Ajay is less sure the lesson has been learned. For individuals, the lesson is to focus on processes and habits, not grand goals.
core_ideas.quote: The truth is we are not pieces on a chessboard that you can make things go the way they want.

core_ideas.concept: The open-ended fallacy and no free lunch
core_ideas.explanation: Health, safety and open space are open-ended desires, but resources are limited and have alternative uses. Amit says India's biggest religion is government: we assume 'mai-baap sarkar' will pay for everything, as if money were unlimited and costless. Yet every government rupee is extracted through taxation, which is coercive and costly, so it has an opportunity cost. Ajay invokes Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch'. A responsible policy thinker should pair every proposal for more spending with matching cuts elsewhere.
core_ideas.quote: Many desirable things are advocated without regard to the most fundamental fact of economics, that resources are inherently limited and have alternative uses.

core_ideas.concept: The sophisticated health expert asks for less government healthcare spending
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay offers a contrarian test of expertise. The Indian government spends poorly, and prevention is better than cure. So the right plea is to reorient the system away from healthcare and towards public health, meaning preventive measures, rather than to demand more money for the same things.
core_ideas.quote: I consider it a hallmark of health expertise in India that the plea of a sophisticated health expert in India should be to cut down government spending on health care.

core_ideas.explanation: Spending is at least capped by what the state can raise. Coercion has no such cap. A government can ban one thing after another and whittle away freedoms day by day with nothing to stop it. So actions that reduce freedom deserve even more scrutiny than actions that cost money.
core_ideas.quote: In spending, there is a budget constraint. It adds up to 100, and you don't have more than 100 rupees to spend. But unfortunately, when it gets to coercion, coercion can be limitless.

core_ideas.concept: Your time is the open-ended fallacy you live with
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's personal version. With age, the binding constraint shifts from money to time. We act under an illusion of immortality and try to give our minds to everything. He cites Steve Jobs's advice to his designer Jonathan Ive: pick a couple of things, say no to the rest, even the ones you love. This is not about a productivity fetish, since time to relax and chill out is useful too.
core_ideas.quote: Learn to say no to things that you love.

core_ideas.explanation: Arnold Kling argues that political tribes talk past each other because their core values differ: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians and classical liberals. Arguing in your own value's language is pointless. Amit gives an example: with a left-winger, he argues that a statist intervention hurts the poor rather than that it reduces freedom. Ajay adds that the sheep come in three flocks, but all share an interest in not being trampled by the wolves.
core_ideas.quote: One way to get past the fighting that we do, this ideological bickering that has become so common, is to recognize the other person's core first principle, which is also to recognize that other person's humanity.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's closing plea. Knowing these fallacies is easy, but internalising them takes a long time. Exam-driven, credential-focused India has a sterile idea of knowledge as a trade you apply, and real reasoning has been pushed out of most people's consciousness. Thinking about thinking is a skill, and it can be learned.
core_ideas.quote: In modern doctor, engineer, MBA, accountant, lawyer India, there is a great crisis of thinking.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The episode opens with both hosts fumbling over who should speak first. Amit turns it into the thesis: 'both of us wanted the other one to go first, and we ended up kind of fighting over it. Not really a fight, but it's a good question. Why do we keep fighting?'
Amit scripts his own cue and Ajay obliges. Amit: 'How does your first fallacy involve hunting? I love it how you follow my instructions and ask me all the questions I want.'

On catching Ryan doing push-ups: 'this goes against the ethical code... thin boys whose bones are visible don't do push-ups.' After hearing the penance explanation: 'in my mind, I did sashtang pranam and I just left.'
Six months later the girls are 'giggling at the improbable presence of a Greek god in their midst... and now I am the only person whose bones are visible.'
Explaining cum hoc ergo propter hoc, Amit admits: 'I love the name because of the main activity in the story.'

On Ajay's biscuit experiment: 'I'm on keto diet, so if I press a button, I don't want a biscuit to come ever. Bacon strips, another matter.' He later reveals his keto plus one-meal-a-day plan: 'because I want to be like Ryan. Which Ryan do I want to be like? Any of the two.'

Amit, on not generalising about economists: 'we know many economists who are sociopaths, Ajay, I want to tell you that, but I know you're not one of them. You're a deeply emotional and empathetic person.'
Amit points to a graph and then corrects himself: 'when I say as you can see, I mean you, gentle reader. He can't see any graph on the screen. There's no screen, there's only me.'
Amit, unabashed: 'I'm gonna be a little vain. I'm gonna name a law of economics after myself because I keep talking about it and no one seems to get it.'

Ajay on investor hubris: the dart-throwing monkey beats nearly all stock pickers, 'Of course, hope springs eternal. We each of us think that I'm in that 0.01% of the cool people that know what to do.'
Ajay teases Amit's claim that India has learned to distrust top-down planning: 'Gentle readers, see how optimistic Amit is.'
In an episode about why we fight, Ajay says Amit opened by 'whining'. Amit: 'I wasn't whining and we will fight over the use of your word whining. I don't whine.'
'PPP: perpetually planned poverty', a phrase coined by the hosts' mutual friend Kumar Anand for what statism and zero-sum thinking produce.
'Mai-baap sarkar kar degi' (the parent-government will provide). Amit says India's 'biggest religion is government', the mindset that powers the open-ended fallacy.
Adam Ferguson's phrase that things happen through 'human action, but not human design', invoked with Hayek to describe spontaneous order.
Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch', Ajay's shorthand for the fact that government money is neither free nor infinite.
Robert Trivers's work on altruism and self-interest, cited by Amit to argue that we are hardwired for both, and that being altruistic indirectly serves our self-interest.

'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will', the phrase Amit uses to answer the gloom: we see what is wrong but keep fighting. He followed it with 'Everything is everything' and then admitted it 'was a dramatic way to end the chapter'.
